Seminar Title:

A Climate-Responsive Compound Flooding Framework for Urban Waterlogging Assessment and Mitigation in Deltaic Cities

Seminar Type:

Registration Seminar

Department:

Civil Engineering

Speaker Name:

Prachi Pragyan Mahanta ( Rollno : 524ce6014)

Speaker Type:

Venue:

Seminar Room Civil Engineering Department NIT Rourkela

Date and Time:

05 Aug 2026 11.00AM

Contact:

Ratnakar Swain

Abstract:

Urban waterlogging is among the most pervasive and economically destructive consequences of rapid urbanization in low-lying deltaic cities, where climate-intensified rainfall, shallow groundwater tables, and river-controlled drainage outfalls interact to produce compound flooding that conventional stationary design cannot capture. This study aims to develop an integrated modelling framework for assessing and mitigating compound pluvial&ndashfluvial waterlogging under present and future climate scenarios by coupling a climate-responsive Non-Stationary Generalised Extreme Value (NS-GEV) design-rainfall model with 1D&ndash2D InfoWorks ICM hydrodynamic simulation, MODFLOW-based groundwater-table zoning, and NSGA-III multi-objective optimization, applied to the shallow-groundwater deltaic city of Cuttack (192.5 km&sup2) in the Mahanadi Delta, India. Daily precipitation from 15 CMIP6 GCMs was bias-corrected using Quantile Delta Mapping against IMD gridded observations (1951&ndash2014), correcting an annual-maximum-series underestimation of approximately 57%. Using four ETCCDI extreme-precipitation indices within an Entropy-TOPSIS framework, five GCMs were selected, with EC-Earth3 identified as the most suitable model (closeness coefficient = 0.983). An NS-GEV model with Global Mean Surface Temperature as a physical covariate was fitted under SSP58.5, and the Mann Kendall test confirmed no significant historical trend (&tau = &minus0.030, p = 0.704), justifying the covariate-based approach. Non-stationary IDF curves were derived at six warming levels (+0.6 &degC to +4.5 &degC). A formal duration-scaling non-stationarity test demonstrated that the conventional stationary scaling exponent underestimates short-duration intensities by up to 56% at +3.0 &degC, degrading the current 50-year design storm to a 24.9-year event (50.2% protection erosion). Climate-responsive Chicago design hyetographs were subsequently generated. The next phase of the research will focus on developing compound pluvial-fluvial 1D&ndash2D simulation with dynamic real-time sluice-gate control, groundwater-constrained NSGA-III spatial optimization of stormwater storage, and evaluation of grey green-blue infrastructure and bioretention systems for sustainable, climate-resilient waterlogging management.
